title: pkix-difftest ignores limbo's expected_peer_name, so all 2895 ground-truth disagreements are phantom
description:
Every single ground-truth disagreement in the x509-limbo run is the same documented harness limitation. Measured against the pinned corpus (third_party/x509-limbo @ b1242378), pkix-path-only:

  9731 in-scope testcases
  2895 ground-truth disagreements
  2894 of them pkix-path says pass where limbo says FAILURE
  2895 of them -- all of them -- carry an expected_peer_name or
       expected_peer_names that the loader deserialises and ignores
     0 disagreements remain once those are set aside

By family: 2836 bettertls (overwhelmingly bettertls::nameconstraints::*), 34 webpki, 24 rfc5280, 1 cve.

The limitation is already written down in corpus/limbo.rs's module docs: 'expected_peer_name / expected_peer_names are deserialised but currently ignored. The harness has no SAN-matching oracle yet.' What was not known is that it accounts for 100% of the disagreements, so the limbo ground-truth comparison currently produces no signal about pkix-path at all -- a ~30% disagreement rate that is entirely harness.

Example: bettertls::nameconstraints::tc10 expects FAILURE with expected_peer_name DNS test.localhost. The chain is structurally valid and pkix-path accepts it, correctly, because nothing told it which name was requested. BetterTLS's nameconstraints suite is specifically about checking the *requested* name against the CA's nameConstraints, not merely the SANs the leaf happens to carry.

This is the same defect shape as PKIX-zd45, closed in 3e9bd47c: a corpus field parsed and never read, turning a harness gap into what reads as the implementation disagreeing with the standard. Worth looking for others of this shape -- limbo.rs documents three more inert fields (signature_algorithms, key_usage, extended_key_usage) and a multi-anchor limitation that only uses trusted_certs[0].

The pieces to wire it up exist. pkix-path already enforces nameConstraints -- PKITS §4.13 is the name-constraints section and all of it agrees with NIST -- and pkix-identity does SAN matching (verify_dns_name, verify_mailbox). What is missing is the harness carrying the requested name to the oracle, the way Chain::initial_policy_inputs now carries the §6.1.1 inputs and Chain::validation_time_unix carries the clock.

Shape of the fix:

1. Carry the expected peer name(s) on Chain, defaulting to none.
2. Populate from limbo's expected_peer_name / expected_peer_names. Both exist; the plural form needs a decision about whether all must match or any.
3. In the pkix-path oracle, after path validation succeeds, check the leaf against the requested name and fail the verdict if it does not match.
4. Decide the same cross-oracle question PKIX-zd45 answered: openssl verify has -verify_hostname and pyca's PolicyBuilder takes a subject, so here all three oracles can probably comply -- which would be better than the per-oracle abstention used for policy inputs. Confirm before assuming.
5. Re-baseline deliberately, with all three oracles.

Until it is wired, consider withholding ground truth for testcases carrying an expected peer name, which is the interim fix PKIX-zd45 used: it keeps the disagreement count honest instead of reporting 2895 implementation defects that are not there. Note that this would withhold ground truth from ~30% of the corpus, which is a large enough share that the interim fix may be worse than the status quo if it makes the corpus look clean when it is merely unmeasured.
close_reason:
Done in 290f66f8. 2895 ground-truth disagreements became 51.

Chain::expected_peer_names carries the identities, the limbo loader populates them from both expected_peer_name and expected_peer_names, and the pkix-path oracle checks the leaf with pkix_identity::verify_dns_name after path validation succeeds. ServerName::parse handles DNS and IP alike, which covers both kinds the corpus uses (5341 and 4455 at the pinned commit). An unparseable identity fails rather than being skipped, since a dropped identity turns an expected rejection into a pass -- the exact failure mode this bead was about.

On the cross-oracle question in step 4: added OracleName::honours_peer_identity and made openssl and pyca abstain, mirroring the policy-inputs gate. The bead's guess was right that all three could comply -- openssl has -verify_hostname and -verify_ip, pyca's PolicyBuilder takes the subject -- so this abstention is a staging point rather than a ceiling, and is noted as such in the method's docs.

Took the plural form as conjunctive: every listed identity must match, because expected_peer_names lists identities a verifier is required to accept, so one that fails is a failure of the testcase. Only 10 testcases use it.

Did not re-baseline. Baselines were taken with three oracles and re-taking needs the pyca sidecar and a ~14 minute run.

The 51 remaining are real signal and want triage, which is not this bead:

  22  webpki::*          (9 cn, 5 aki, 2 nc, and singletons) -- limbo's
                         webpki namespace encodes strictness RFC 5280
                         does not require, so some of these are likely
                         legitimate policy differences rather than bugs
  22  rfc5280::*         (5 nc, 3 aki, 3 ski, 2 eku, 2 san, and
                         singletons). Four are about the trust anchor's
                         own extensions -- root-missing-basic-
                         constraints, root-non-critical-basic-
                         constraints, root-inconsistent-ca-extensions,
                         unknown-critical-extension-root -- where §6.1
                         deliberately processes nothing, so those are
                         probably a deliberate divergence to document
   6  bettertls::pathbuilding -- all expect FAILURE with peer localhost
   1  cve::cve-2025-61727 -- filed as PKIX-bhtl, P1

Direction is 50 pass-where-failure-expected and 1 the other way.

PKIX-bhtl is the one that matters: a wildcard SAN evades a dNSName name constraint, because path validation compares the literal string *.example.com against the excluded subtree while pkix-identity then matches the requested name against the wildcard. An ICA forbidden from bar.example.com successfully certifies a cert that authenticates bar.example.com. pkix-path has always behaved that way; it became visible only once the harness started asking the identity question, which is the argument for having wired it.
